scenario.title: Fading Dials, Hybrid Signals
scenario.setting: KWTL-92.3 Community Radio occupies a converted 1980s fire station annex in the western Appalachian foothills. It operates as a network of volunteer cells: on-air rotation, engineering maintenance, fundraising outreach, and community booking. Sustained by a small core crew of 8 active volunteers, the station has operated past its first full decade of service. Over the past decade, its terrestrial listenership has dropped by exactly half, as locals now prioritize online streaming and social media instead of tuning into terrestrial dials.

characters.name: Marisol Cruz
characters.tendencies: She is the station's lead manager, overseeing all volunteer cells and coordinating grant applications and emergency broadcast schedules. She has spent the past three years leading grant-writing and organizing pledge drives to reverse the station's declining listenership.

characters.name: Lila Mae Jenkins
characters.tendencies: She hosts the weekly Local Folk Hour, inviting local farmers, poets, and retirees to share their work and stories. She has noticed her core regular listeners are mostly over 65, and struggles to recruit younger volunteers or listeners for her show or the station overall.

characters.name: Jai Reddy
characters.tendencies: He is the station's volunteer data auditor, compiling monthly listenership metrics and quarterly reports for the crew. He tracks both terrestrial radio and online stream numbers, identifying gaps in the station's outreach and audience engagement.

characters.name: Eddie "Tink" Marlow
characters.tendencies: He is a retired ham radio operator and volunteer engineering cell member, tinkering with the station's aging broadcast tower and transmitter hardware. He has recently developed a hybrid terrestrial-online broadcast setup that has started drawing a small new cohort of young listeners.

turns.name: Lila Mae Jenkins
turns.text:
Good evening, KWTL-92.3 Local Folk Hour crew. I’m putting out an extra call this week to folks under 30—whether you pen poems about the creek behind your dorm, grow tomatoes on your apartment fire escape, or sell homemade pickles at the downtown farmers market, we want your voice on our airwaves. No fancy experience needed, just a story or small local tune you’re excited to share.
[leans in to tweak the studio mic’s volume dial, then plucks a crumpled handwritten note slipped under the studio door earlier and tucks it into the wooden contributor sign-up binder atop the soundboard]

turns.name: Jai Reddy
turns.text:
I just finished tallying this month’s terrestrial and online listenership metrics, and we’ve seen an 8% jump in local trucker listeners tuning in during overnight shifts. I also flagged a gap in our weekend youth programming that several middle school callers mentioned during last week’s open request line.
[jots a quick reminder to loop in the programming volunteer coordinator before tucking his spiral-bound report under his arm]

turns.name: Eddie "Tink" Marlow
turns.text:
That aging 1972 transmitter tube’s definitely on its last legs—figured I’d swap it out before those new young listeners tune in for the post-hike folk block later. Don’t want their first taste of community radio to be nothing but fizzing static and creaky tower hum.
[leans up to twist a loose grounding screw tight on the tower’s lower boom assembly]

turns.name: Lila Mae Jenkins
turns.text:
Chuckling at Tink’s quick fix forecast, I lean forward on the scuffed control booth desk. We’ve got to meet those young listeners halfway—why not let them host a 15-minute pre-block spot while you pop that new tube in, Eddie? I’ve got a pile of student poetry zines from the local community college right here, all full of mountain-adjacent stories just like we love.
[reaches for a neon-pink stapled zine tucked under a stack of worn broadcast logs]

turns.name: Jai Reddy
turns.text: That 8% jump among local truckers lines up perfectly with the overnight tire shop roundup updates we launched last month, and the outreach gap I flagged earlier is exactly the under-30 demographic you’re highlighting tonight. [taps the edge of his dog-eared listenership spreadsheet before nodding toward Eddie’s work by the transmitter bay]

turns.name: Eddie "Tink" Marlow
turns.text: Don’t want their first taste of community radio to be crackling static instead of Darryl’s fiddle cuts. I pulled the spare 1972-spec transmitter tube from the ham shack storage bin last week, just waiting for this exact fizzle-out. [kneels beside the buzzing transmitter rack, using a flathead screwdriver to pry loose the corroded old tube housing]
